title: Event Studies in Economics and Finance
research_question: Do quarterly earnings announcements convey value-relevant information to investors, such that unexpected components of announced earnings are reflected in the equity values of announcing firms around the announcement date?
data_description: The illustrative sample consists of quarterly earnings announcements for the 30 firms in the Dow Jones Industrial Index over the five-year period from January 1989 through December 1993, covering earnings for the last quarter of 1988 through the third quarter of 1993, yielding 600 firm-quarter announcements. For each announcement, three pieces of information are compiled: the announcement date (from Datastream), the actual reported earnings (from Compustat), and a measure of expected earnings proxied by the mean analyst forecast from the Institutional Brokers Estimate System (I/B/E/S), taken from the last month of the relevant quarter. Daily stock returns are used, with a 41-day window around each announcement (20 days before, the announcement day, and 20 days after) and a 250 trading-day pre-announcement period. The CRSP value-weighted index serves as the market portfolio. Announcements are sorted into good news (189), no news (173), and bad news (238) based on whether actual earnings exceed, fall within 2.5%, or fall short of expected earnings.
institutional_context: The Financial Accounting Standards Board and the Securities and Exchange Commission set reporting regulations with the goal of ensuring that financial statements and related disclosures convey information useful for valuing firms. Quarterly earnings announcements are a recurring, regulated disclosure through which publicly traded U.S. corporations release accounting information to investors. Because firms in the Dow Jones Industrial Index are widely followed by financial analysts, analyst-based consensus forecasts (such as those compiled by I/B/E/S) provide a market-based benchmark of prior expectations against which the actual reported figure can be compared. If these mandated disclosures genuinely add information beyond what investors already anticipate, then surprises relative to consensus expectations should be associated with revaluations of the firm's equity at the time of release, while announcements that merely confirm expectations should produce little reaction.
